description: Georgia's Return to Play Act of 2013 requires all public and private schools to adopt a concussion management and return to play policy.
shortAnswer: The Return to Play Act of 2013 mandates that all public and private schools must adopt and implement a concussion management and return to play policy. The rationale behind the law is that school officials are in the best position to prevent children and teens from returning to play after a blow to the head.

faq.q: What does Georgia's Return to Play Act require schools to do?
faq.a: Schools must provide written warnings to coaches, students and parents about the risks of concussion and head injury prior to the start of each athletic season, require each coach to complete an annual concussion recognition course, and require coaches and school officials to comply with a uniform return to play protocol.

faq.q: Can I sue a Georgia school if a coach let my child keep playing after a concussion?
faq.a: The answer is unfortunately complex. If your child is injured while attending public schools your rights are fewer than if the injury happens at a private school. The question is whether the Courts will interpret the new duties as ministerial (no immunity) or discretionary (immunity), and it is unknown how the Courts will interpret this new law.

faq.q: Are the duties under Georgia's Return to Play Act ministerial or discretionary?
faq.a: I believe the Courts should interpret the duties under the new law as ministerial. No discretion is needed: the coach or school official needs to remove the child from play and not allow return to play until the appropriate health provider has examined the child and cleared them to return.
